Research Log: Phenomenon-Driven Instructional Framework

Table of Contents

  • Executive Summary
  • Part I: Instructional Framework
  • Part II: Implementation Guidelines
  • Part III: Meeting Minutes & Documentation
  • Part IV: Practical Resources
  • Appendix: Problem Set Exemplars

Executive Summary

This document outlines a systematic framework and practical workflow for designing phenomenon-driven curriculum. It supports professional development teams in applying a consistent, inquiry-based instructional model across various courses. The core principle is to begin with the end goal—deep student understanding—and work backward to create a coherent, engaging, and compelling course of study.

Part I: The Instructional Framework This framework is built upon a core narrative that organizes content, a clear structure that guides student inquiry, and a set of practical tools for classroom implementation.

  1. Core Philosophy: A Narrative Approach This curriculum is built on a simple idea: students should figure things out for themselves, not just memorize facts from a book. Every unit begins with a real-world phenomenon—a compelling event or puzzle—that gives students a genuine reason to ask questions. This approach connects the science directly to the world students live in, showing how it applies to both local and global challenges. The learning process is about building understanding over time. Students create initial models or explanations, test them against new information, and revise them as they learn more. It is a continuous cycle of thinking and rethinking.

The narrative voice is a synthesis of three key intellectual influences:

From James Burke (The Web of Connections): The voice adopts a narrative, storytelling approach that reveals the interconnectedness of scientific concepts. This perspective continually asks the fundamental question: “How did we get here, and what does this mean for us?” From Carl Sagan (The Cosmic Perspective): The voice cultivates a profound sense of wonder and awe. This perspective continually asks the fundamental question: “Where are we in the great cosmic ocean, and how does this knowledge make our lives more meaningful?” From Richard Feynman (The Joy of Finding Things Out): The voice embraces an infectious curiosity and a playful spirit of inquiry. This perspective continually asks the fundamental question: “What are the rules of the game? And is it not a joy to figure them out?” This philosophy is put into practice through a central story that provides a coherent structure for complex topics. In physics, for example, this is “A Story of Matter, Energy, and Force.” This narrative can be introduced as follows:

At its heart, the story of physics is a grand investigation with three main characters. Everything that happens in the universe is a result of the intricate and often dramatic ways these three interact.

Matter: The Protagonist. Matter is the “who” of our story. It is all the tangible substance, from a single atom to a sprawling galaxy. It possesses inertia, a stubborn reluctance to change its state of motion. Matter is the physical stage and all the actors upon it. Energy: The Plot. Energy is the “what happens” in our story. It is the universe’s currency for change, a restless agent that is never created or destroyed, only transformed. Without Energy, the story would be a single, static frame. Force: The Director. Force is the “how” and “why” of our story. It is the interaction, the push and pull between objects of Matter. It is the messenger that “tells” Matter how to move and the agent that allows Energy to be transferred. Force directs all the action. Instructional Structure: Anchors, Practices and Lenses The curriculum is structured to guide students from concrete observations toward more abstract, principled understanding.

Anchoring Phenomena: Each unit is anchored by a compelling, real-world phenomenon or puzzle. This serves as the central focus for all learning activities, providing a consistent “need to know” that drives student inquiry. They orient the student’s exposure to the Disciplinary Core Ideas to students’ inquiry in compelling and as close to authentic contexts as possible. Practices - The 8 Practices of the NGSS guide what students do with the phenomena. Designing experiments could consist of various Elements with different numbers of chunks, offset perhaps by Constructing Explanations of those experiments in a later Element. Crosscutting Concepts as “Lenses”: The seven NGSS Crosscutting Concepts (e.g., Cause and Effect, Systems and System Models) are used as explicit “thinking lenses.” Each unit is guided by one of these concepts, helping students organize their knowledge and make connections across different domains. Elements - are the content-agnostic, chunkable activities that use a Crosscutting Concept to lens a Practice. The element simply makes thinking visible while students engage with the Practice. It is an artifact of focus for reflection and assessment. It exists as a Google Doc with prompts, tasks, and templates to structure and organize student thinking. These are highly adaptable in complexity, length, reading-level, cognitive task, and modality (i.e. a physical model is still an invaluable learning experience, but an image or schematic of the model can exist in the Research Log for later review). Megacognitive Prompts - They link a specific activity or problem back to a student’s overall understanding or a particular learning strategy. They extend and connect numerical answers, and encourage students to think about how they arrived at their solutions. When possible, they explore connections between units (i.e. in a previous chapter we looked at movement due to forces. Compare that to our present examination of potential and kinetic energy. What are two strengths of each conceptual model?). The metacognitive prompts act as the throughthread between segments of the Problem Sets as they gradually increase in complexity and cognitive load. Artifacts

A set of consistent, student-facing tools is used to make the inquiry process visible and structured.

The Research Brief: A comprehensive digital document that guides students through an investigation. It includes metacognitive checkpoints at the beginning (“Forecast”), middle (“Blueprint”), and end (“Reflection”) of a learning cycle to promote self-awareness and strategic thinking. Resource Materials: These are embedded into the Flexbook and are completed during the Research portions of the students’ unit chunks.

Phenomenon Decks: Resources that introduce the central phenomenon through narratives, images, and initial data. Slide Decks - HTML marp markdown.md files, to accompany Lectures. Structured to integrate with Cornell Notes hard copies for students. Problem Sets - HTML files with dynamic data representation and computational practice problems. These guide student Concept and Computational Time between Lectures. Hexagon Laboratories: Curated collections of datasets, mock scientific papers, and other resources that students analyze to solve the central puzzle. Instructional Workflow

Aligning Time with Purpose The framework requires a purposeful allocation of classroom time and a structured feedback cycle to ensure a productive and effective learning environment.

Time Allocation: Daily instruction is reallocated to distinct “Research” and “Practice” blocks. This provides dedicated time for student-led inquiry and skill development. Feedback Cycle: Each strand or segment (Forecast, Blueprint, Reflection) occupies its own Google Doc. All three strands comprise the Research Log for that Chapter. Each Brief contains at least three pages: Prompt, where system prompts by the instructor and students are defined; Content, where the student answers and annotations reside; Appendix, where the transcript of the AI conversation(s) (if any) that apply to that segment are stored. Foundational Commitments: Equity and Empathy The curriculum is built upon a commitment to equitable access and empathy-forward discussion, which are integrated into the instructional design. Empathy in Application: When addressing phenomena with real-world consequences, instruction is delivered with sensitivity. The focus is on demonstrating how scientific understanding can be used to design safer and more just solutions for all communities. Computational Empathy: Computational exploration is leveraged to foster compassionate citizenship. Students calculate the impacts of engineering or infrastructure decisions, connecting computational thinking with empathetic thought to highlight the real-world implications of science. Development Phase

Phase 1: Solidifying the Foundation (Now - Fall 2025)

Objective: To create a stable, replicable framework for a single subject (Physics) that can serve as a template for all others. The focus is on processes, not just content.

Action Steps:

Finalize the Core Document Set: Create a single “Master Template” for the curriculum, incorporating the “storyline” and “human element” concepts you’ve already discussed. Formalize the research-log.html and curriculum.json files as the official, living documents for the course. Write a clear, simple guide on how to update and maintain these two files. Pilot and Refine the Workflow: Run the Google Classroom workflow you’ve already defined for the first full unit of your physics class. Use the AI-assisted data analysis process after the first major quiz. The goal isn’t just to get data, but to refine the prompts and process itself. At the end of the unit, hold a small team meeting to discuss what worked, what didn’t, and why. This is your chance to iterate on the process. Create a Training “Package”: Document the entire process—from idea to implementation—in a clear, non-technical format. Use a simple, shared Google Doc or folder. This is the foundation for your future professional development. The package should include: A one-page summary of the core philosophy. A checklist for setting up a new unit. Templates for the research-log.html and curriculum.json files. A guide to the Google Classroom workflow. Phase 2: Expanding the Blueprint (Spring 2026 - Summer 2026)

Objective: To prove that the system is content-agnostic and to create the infrastructure for digital publishing.

Action Steps:

Choose a Second Subject Team: Identify a second department (e.g., Biology, History, English) that is interested in a similar curriculum redesign. The goal is to test the system’s flexibility. Can the “storyline,” “phenomenon-driven,” and “Research Log” concepts be applied to the Civil War or Shakespeare? Develop a Digital Publishing Workflow: Work with your IT department to set up a simple hosting solution. This could be a static website generator like Jekyll or just a shared folder on a web server. The goal is to connect the curriculum.json data to a web page. When you update the JSON file, the website should update automatically. This will require some basic web development skills, but it’s a key step for creating dynamic content. Run the Pilot with the Second Team: Guide the new team through the process using the training package you created in Phase 1. Hold regular check-ins to identify where the process needs to be adjusted for a different subject. What language needs to change? What does a “phenomenon” look like in a history class? Document the lessons learned. Phase 3: Scaling and Sustaining (Fall 2026 and Beyond)

Objective: To fully implement the system across multiple departments and to create a sustained, long-term support model.

Action Steps:

Roll Out the System: Schedule professional development sessions for other interested departments using the training package. Create “Department Champions”—one person from each team who is an expert in the system and can answer basic questions. Build a Centralized Curriculum Database: Merge the individual curriculum.json files into one master database. Create a simple search interface so any teacher can search for a lesson or activity by topic, skill, or NGSS standard, regardless of which department created it. This fosters cross-curricular collaboration. Formalize the Workflow: Establish a regular cycle for curriculum review and update. This includes scheduled meetings to analyze data from quizzes and student feedback to make informed decisions about content. The goal is to move from a one-time project to a standard, school-wide practice. Meeting Minutes

Of course. Here is a summary of our collaborative process, its evolution, and the final determinations we’ve made for your course design.

Original Intention: Content Creation We began with a clear and focused goal: to draft the chapter-by-chapter content for a new “Natural Hazard Engineering” flexbook. The initial parameters were well-defined:

A Narrative Voice: The “Historian of Human Ingenuity,” inspired by Sagan and Burke. A Core Structure: A three-role model (Scientist -> Engineer -> Policymaker) centered on a Branford, CT case study. A Target Audience: High school non-science majors. Our process was iterative, focusing on drafting one chapter at a time, incorporating feedback, and then moving to the next.

The Evolution: From Content to Pedagogy Our collaboration quickly evolved beyond simple content drafting into a comprehensive design of the entire learning experience. Key shifts in our thinking included:

The Research Brief as a “Spinal Column”: The most significant evolution was the creation of the “Research Brief.” This transformed the three main artifacts (Risk Report, Engineering Proposal, Policy Brief) from separate assignments into a single, cumulative portfolio. This decision made the course’s core philosophy—the flow of information from one role to the next—a tangible, central part of the student workflow. Formalizing the “Rhythm” of a Lesson: We moved from a general list of activities to a highly specific, repeatable pedagogical sequence for each chapter. This established a clear rhythm for your teaching: Hook (metacognition/emotion) -> Inquire (peer discussion) -> Acquire (reading) -> Clarify (lecture) -> Check (quiz) -> Apply (Hexagon Labs) -> Synthesize (artifact creation). Deepening the Narrative: We made several key refinements to the content to strengthen the narrative, such as changing the “heat engine” analogy to a “thermal flywheel” for clarity and integrating the powerful “space vs. place” concept to add sociological depth to the policy debates. Defining Your Teaching Philosophy: Our process culminated in a meta-discussion where we synthesized your entire approach into a detailed system prompt for an AI assistant. This shifted our focus from just creating your course to creating a tool that can help you create like you. Final Determinations: A Complete Blueprint Through this process, we’ve arrived at a comprehensive and robust blueprint for the “Natural Hazard Engineering” course. The final determinations include:

A Complete Content Draft: We have a full draft of the flexbook text, including 12 core chapters, a concluding chapter, and all associated appendices for four distinct units. A Detailed Workflow: We have a clear, step-by-step pedagogical sequence that maps out the student experience for every chapter. A Logistical Plan: We determined the most effective way to manage the course using a structured Google Doc template for the Research Brief, managed through multiple, distinct assignments in Google Classroom to ensure clear grading and pacing. A Guiding Philosophy: The ultimate goal of the course was clarified: to cultivate civic responsibility, an appreciation for complexity, and a desire for informed participation in real-world decision-making. This provides a clear “north star” for all future lesson design. Lecture notes: I’m glad to help you reflect on your workflow. Based on our conversation, here is a summary of our process and how the lesson design evolved.

Initial Intent & First Draft You first requested a set of lecture notes for Chapter 5 focused on coastal and volcanic resilience. My initial draft included content on volcanoes, which you corrected to be specifically about tsunamis and early warning systems. This highlighted the importance of a clear and focused thematic approach for each chapter.

Refinement and Iteration As we continued, we made several key adjustments:

Activity Removal: We removed the activity sections (e.g., “Mitigation Design Challenge”) from the notes themselves, as they are introduced elsewhere in your curriculum. This clarified the document’s purpose as a lecture handout. Content Alignment: I made an error by including concepts related to earthquakes in a chapter on coastal resilience. You corrected this, reminding me to ensure the content (like materials and structural principles) was specific to tsunamis and storm surges. Redundancy Check: You caught a redundancy where both Chapter 4 and Chapter 5 mentioned DART buoys. This led to a crucial decision to separate the topics: the scientist’s role is to gather data (like from DART buoys), while the engineer’s role is to design the systems that use that data. This was a key insight for maintaining a clear distinction between the roles in each chapter. Final Determination Ultimately, our process led to a clear, iterative workflow:

Start with the Core Concept: Begin with a high-level idea for the chapter (e.g., “Policymaker: Governing the Interface”). Draft and Refine Sections: Break the concept into logical subsections (e.g., Building Codes, Forest Management, etc.) and draft the content. Check for Alignment: Review the new content against the broader curriculum to ensure there are no redundancies and that it aligns with the distinct roles of the scientist, engineer, and policymaker. Confirm the Final Product: The final document serves as a concise, well-organized lecture guide that supports your lesson design without containing extraneous information like activities or learning objectives. This collaborative process of drafting, critiquing, and refining each chapter ensures that the final lesson notes are not only accurate but also perfectly aligned with the nuanced pedagogical philosophy of the “Architect of Understanding.”

The Consequence Engine: Our collaboration began with a focused, tactical request: to add trust and resilience variables to an existing HTML file for a web-based game.

Evolutions in Process The project quickly evolved from a simple data update to a comprehensive lesson design, following these key phases:

From Static Data to Interactive Web Prototype: We began by adding variables to a static HTML page, then made it interactive by adding JavaScript to reveal the values on a button click. This confirmed the core mechanic would work. From Web Prototype to Data-Driven Game Concept: The project’s scope expanded with the creation of a centralized .json file to house all game variables (towns, scenarios, impacts, and solutions). This established a flexible, scalable architecture for the game’s data, allowing for easy modifications. From Simple Mechanics to Strategic Complexity: We then introduced a brainstorming phase to add “spice” to the game’s mechanics. The initial ideas for complex modifiers were simplified based on your feedback to a more approachable “Monopoly-style” chance card system, creating a fun, binary modifier for each solution. From Web-Based to Spreadsheet-Based Design: The most significant evolution was the pivot from designing a web game to drafting a Google Sheets-based interactive game board. This required translating web development logic into spreadsheet formulas, demonstrating the core game concept can be taught on different platforms. Final Determinations Our final workflow has resulted in a well-documented, multi-platform lesson plan. We have created:

A full-fledged, data-rich game concept: The Resilience & Trust game, complete with all variables and modifiers necessary for a fully functional simulation. A detailed data backend: A comprehensive .json file and a corresponding Google Sheets data table that houses all game variables. Multiple user interfaces: We drafted HTML pages for an introductory experience and a modifier reference, and designed a functional game board using Google Sheets with all necessary formulas. An educational framework: We concluded by drafting a summary document that explains the game’s core concepts and provides an analytical example, effectively turning the project into a comprehensive, ready-to-use lesson plan for educators. This process demonstrates how starting with a simple idea, then incrementally adding complexity based on user needs, can lead to a robust and highly adaptable final product that serves multiple pedagogical goals.

Architecture

Conversation Summary: Flexbook Unit Design Workflow Our conversation began with the goal of refining the introductory text for a high school natural hazard engineering unit. The initial document was a detailed philosophical and pedagogical blueprint.

Initial Intentions Our primary objective was to draft the introductory chapter for the Flexbook, serving as the foundation for a semester-long curriculum. This introduction was meant to:

Introduce the concept of geo-literacy. Establish a narrative arc for students transitioning between the roles of Scientist, Engineer, and Policymaker. Define the Consequence Engine, a core framework for understanding tradeoffs. Introduce the philosophical distinction between space and place. Key Evolutions & Iterations The conversation evolved through several key refinements, driven by a shared goal of simplifying complex ideas for a 10th-grade audience:

Simplifying the Consequence Engine: The initial variables for the “Consequence Engine” were too academic (“Epistemic Reliability,” “Fiscal Stewardship”). We iteratively simplified them into more accessible terms like “Trust in Science,” “Financial Cost,” and “Fairness & Equity.” This process underscored the importance of translating academic concepts into a relatable language. Harmonizing Roles: We recognized that the Engineer and Policymaker were too siloed. We integrated the concepts of “Longevity” and “Cost of Inaction” into the Engineer’s role, directly connecting their design choices to the Policymaker’s long-term financial and social responsibilities. This created a more harmonious and realistic model. Adding a “Space vs. Place” Section: To bridge the gap between the abstract Consequence Engine and the human element, we introduced a new section. This segment helps students understand how a neutral, physical location (space) gains meaning and value (place) through human history and professional analysis. Integrating Prompts: We integrated comprehension and metacognitive prompts directly into the document. This ensures that the reflective “think about your thinking” component of the course is a central part of the text, not just a separate activity. Final Determinations & Optimized Workflow The final, optimized workflow for lesson design emerged from these iterations. Instead of a linear, one-and-done process, our conversation demonstrated a cyclical, iterative design loop.

Start with the Core Idea: Begin with a high-level philosophical blueprint. Draft a Foundational Document: Create the primary text that embodies this philosophy. Iterate and Simplify: Ruthlessly simplify and refine the language and concepts to fit the target audience. Add Interconnecting Bridges: Build new sections or ideas to connect seemingly disparate concepts, creating a more cohesive and synthesized learning experience. Embed Assessment & Reflection: Integrate questions and prompts directly into the content to encourage metacognition and practical application from the very first draft. This process ensures that the final product is not just accurate, but also pedagogically sound, accessible, and deeply aligned with the original curriculum’s mission.

Research Briefs

Our conversation began with your request to brainstorm a set of metacognitive prompts, or “Research Briefs,” to help your high school physics students reflect on their learning111. We started with an example from a 2D Kinematics unit2.

The conversation evolved into a broader discussion about how to integrate these briefs into your specific

Natural Hazard Engineering curriculum3. I proposed three frameworks:

Unit-Specific: Aligning briefs with specific unit content. Routine & Rhythmic: Using the same briefs at predictable intervals across all units. Portfolio-Driven: Making briefs building blocks for a final portfolio. Our final determination centered on the

“Routine & Rhythmic” framework as the optimal choice for your situation4. This decision was based on its beneficial predictability for students 5and its ease of implementation for a solo instructor with a tight deadline6. This approach directly supports your learning objective of helping students become better learners through consistent, ritualized self-reflection7.

We then drafted a concise implementation timeline and a set of sample prompts for this framework8. The final architecture of the briefs is a three-part system: “The Forecast” (pre-unit), “The Blueprint” (problem-solving), and “The Reflection” (post-unit)9.

Meeting Minutes Topic: Curriculum Development Day: Physics Textbook Table of Contents Review Date: 08/19/2025 Objective: To refine and finalize the structure, flow, and content of the introductory physics textbook’s table of contents. Summary of Proceedings The session began with a review of the draft table of contents (ToC). A series of iterative changes were discussed and implemented to improve the document’s educational effectiveness and narrative cohesion. Key Decisions and Action Items Integration of Concepts and Computations: Discussion: The initial format listed key concepts and computations in a summary at the end of each chapter. It was agreed that this separated theory from application. Decision: The ToC was restructured to integrate computations and formulas directly into the relevant subsections. This change creates a more natural learning progression, where a concept is introduced and immediately followed by its mathematical application. Modernizing Application Examples: Discussion: The capstone example for Chapter 10, “How a Photocopier Works,” was identified as outdated and less engaging for today’s students. Decision: The example was replaced with “How a Smartphone Touchscreen Works” to provide a modern, relevant application of electrostatic principles. Rebalancing Chapter 10 Content: Discussion: The team noted that Chapter 10 was overly focused on electrostatics and lacked a proper introduction to basic circuits. A foundational understanding of current, voltage, and simple circuits was deemed essential for an introductory course. Decision: Chapter 10 was significantly revised and retitled “Electricity: From Sparks to Circuits.” The new structure introduces static charge and Coulomb’s Law, then transitions to flowing charge (current, voltage, resistance), Ohm’s Law, and concludes with an analysis of simple series and parallel circuits. The “Smartphone Touchscreen” example was retained as the capstone, as it effectively bridges both static and circuit concepts. Narrative and Phrasing Enhancements: Discussion: A final pass was conducted to improve the titles and descriptive language throughout the ToC to make the material more engaging and intuitive. Decision: Minor copy edits were approved to enhance the narrative flow (e.g., renaming “A Cast of Forces” to “Identifying the Players”). Outcome The table of contents is now considered final. The revised structure provides a clear and logical path for students, effectively weaving together narrative phenomena, investigation, and computational physics. Meeting Minutes: Physics Curriculum Development Date: 8/19/2025 Topic: Framework and initial design for a new, NGSS-aligned introductory physics course. Lead: E. Ainsworth

1.0 Project Goal & Core Philosophy Objective: Develop a new, phenomenon-driven physics curriculum and accompanying “Flexbook” text. Core Narrative: Unifying theme is the story of Matter (the protagonist), Energy (the plot), and Forces (the director). Pedagogy: Must be NGSS-aligned, focusing on student “figuring out” over memorization. All units anchored in observable phenomena. Target Audience: 9-12th grade, general to honors level. 2.0 “Flexbook Voice” & Tone Decision: Adopt a synthesized voice combining three key influences: James Burke: Emphasize interconnectedness, historical context, and narrative. Carl Sagan: Cultivate cosmic perspective and a sense of wonder. Richard Feynman: Foster playful inquiry and a reverence for the elegance of underlying rules. Action Item: All generated text to adhere to this established voice. 3.0 Curriculum Structure & Narrative Arc Decision: A 3-Part, 10-Chapter structure was developed. Part I (Ch. 1-3): Learning the Language of Nature. Theme: From subjective description to objective quantification. Focus: Kinematics, measurement, vectors. Part II (Ch. 4-7): The Great Unification. Theme: From observation to universal principles. Focus: Dynamics (Newton’s Laws), Energy, Momentum, Gravitation. Part III (Ch. 8-10): The Unseen World. Theme: From the tangible to the abstract. Focus: Waves, Optics, Electrostatics. Key Feature: Each chapter is annotated with a central question, narrative arc, key principles (Giancoli ref.), anchoring phenomena, and explicit links to NGSS Crosscutting Concepts (CCCs). 4.0 NGSS Alignment & Progression Decision: The 3-Part structure is explicitly designed to advance students from Middle School (MS) to High School (HS) performance expectations for Science and Engineering Practices (SEPs) and CCCs. Part I: Advances mathematical/data analysis skills (MS linear -> HS nonlinear). Part II: Advances modeling/explanation skills (MS descriptive -> HS predictive/mathematical models). Part III: Advances abstract thinking & argumentation from indirect evidence. 5.0 Google Classroom Workflow & Implementation Topic: Management of student portfolios (“Research Logs”). Decision: Adopt an “Adaptable Unit-Based Workflow.” Structure: One Google Doc per major “Part” (e.g., Part I covers Ch. 1-3). Distribution: Assign the full template for the Part at the beginning, selecting “Make a copy for each student.” Rationale: Provides flexibility for the instructor to adapt future chapters based on pacing/student needs, while keeping related work organized for students. Topic: Student Accountability & Progress Checks. Decision: Utilize the “Turn In / Return” cycle within Google Classroom. Process: Students “Turn In” the long-term document for periodic checkpoints. Instructor provides feedback and then “Returns” the document, restoring editing access for the next phase of work. Rationale: Creates clear accountability checkpoints without fragmenting the portfolio into multiple assignments. 6.0 Next Steps Three potential paths forward were identified: Develop a Model Unit: Fully build out one complete unit (e.g., Unit 4) as a template. Design Summative Assessments: Detail the major performance-based tasks for the end of each of the three Parts. Create Teacher’s Toolkit for Part I: Develop all practical, ready-to-use instructional materials for the first three chapters. Certainly. I can provide a summary of our conversation in the form of meeting minutes.

Minutes from the Professional Development Session on AI Integration Date: August 19, 2025

Attendees: The instructor and Eleanor Ainsworth

Topic: A Framework for AI Integration in the Classroom

  1. Course Structure & Philosophy:

The core philosophy of the course is to present physics not as a static body of facts but as a dynamic story of inquiry. The structure is built around a student-centric, phenomenon-driven model. The primary tool for this inquiry is the “Research Brief,” a living document where students log observations, questions, and their evolving understanding.

  1. AI Integration Framework:

The group discussed a proposed framework for the responsible integration of AI, predicated on the hypothesis that explicit instruction in prompt generation and metacognitive support will improve student self-knowledge. This framework is organized into three main components:

Norms: The philosophical underpinnings of AI use. Key norms include a commitment to Intellectual Honesty (full transparency in AI use) and the Human-in-the-Loop Principle (students are ultimately responsible for the intellectual content of their work). Tools: Practical elements to facilitate AI integration. These include the Research Brief and Metacognitive Log, a public Library of Inquiries (a directory of prompts), and the Prompt Generator (an activity to teach students how to create their own prompts). Assignments: Specific pedagogical applications of AI. Examples include the “AI is Wrong” Assignment (to teach critical evaluation), the “Intellectual Mirror” Interview (to promote self-knowledge), and the “Explanation Adaptation” Exercise (to teach rhetorical skills).

  1. Action Items:

Formalize the “Research Brief” as a central document. Draft new documentation for the course structure, providing an overview of student activities and learning outcomes for each chapter. Explore and develop the “Library of Inquiries” and “Prompt Generator” as concrete resources for students. Begin planning the first set of AI-integrated assignments. The session concluded with an agreement to move forward with the development of these ideas, with the aim of building a robust system that teaches students how to be responsible and self-aware participants in an increasingly technology-driven world.

This summary serves as the meeting minutes for our professional development session, documenting the collaborative development of a physics curriculum.

Meeting Minutes: Physics Curriculum Development Date: August 19, 2025 Topic: Refinement of the Physics: A Story of Matter, Forces, and Energy Curriculum Schedule Key Decisions & Action Items The primary objective of the session was to refine the existing physics curriculum schedule, moving from a broad outline to a detailed, actionable plan. The following key changes and additions were agreed upon:

Removal of Lecture Blocks: All scheduled “Lecture” time blocks were eliminated. The time was reallocated to “Research” and “Practice” activities to better align with the curriculum’s phenomenon-driven, inquiry-based model. Elaborated Activity Descriptions: Each 20-minute time block was given a more detailed, single-statement description of the activity. This includes specific references to “Hexagon Labs,” “Claim, Evidence, and Reasoning (CER)” arguments, and “problem sets,” providing a clear understanding of student engagement for each unit. Anchoring Phenomena: Each of the ten units was anchored to a specific, real-world phenomenon. The team adopted the benchmark phenomena from the provided Benchmark Phenomena for Physics Assessment document to ensure consistency between instruction and assessment. This decision reinforces the central philosophy of the curriculum. Cross-Cutting Concepts: A specific “Cross-Cutting Concept” from the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) was assigned to each unit. This provides an overarching conceptual framework for the content, connecting disparate physics topics through a shared intellectual lens. Detailed Data Descriptions: A new data entry line was added to each unit’s “Research” section, detailing the specific type of data students will be provided to analyze. This ensures the curriculum has a clear and practical plan for the hands-on, data-driven nature of the research blocks. Problem Set Brainstorm: A list of three to five specific problem sets was brainstormed for each “Practice” block. These problem sets are concisely described with single-statement headings, providing concrete examples of how students will apply their knowledge through problem-solving. This collaborative effort has successfully transformed the curriculum outline into a well-defined, phenomenon-driven schedule. The detailed minutes reflect the team’s commitment to creating a practical and engaging resource for students.

Curriculum Development Day: AI-Assisted Data Analysis Date: August 19, 2025

Attendees: Instructor, AI Facilitator

Topic: Leveraging AI to Analyze Student Quiz Data and Inform Curriculum Development

  1. Objective & Initial Analysis

The objective was to establish a process for using AI to move beyond basic quiz metrics (e.g., average score) and derive actionable, curriculum-informing insights from student data. The discussion began with an analysis of provided quiz results, which highlighted key areas of student difficulty, particularly related to the electromagnetic spectrum and the application of the wave equation.

  1. Refinement of Approach

The initial set of prompts, while useful for foundational analysis, were deemed too surface-level for instructors already familiar with statistical data. The conversation pivoted to a more advanced application of AI, focusing on how a language model can uncover deeper patterns.

  1. Key Prompts Developed

The following three-step process and corresponding prompts were developed to guide the analysis:

Step 1: Data Provision: Instructors must export Google Form quiz responses as a CSV file for AI analysis. Step 2: Strategic Prompting: Prompts were categorized for clarity and purpose: Foundational Analysis: Concise prompts for core metrics (e.g., “Summarize quiz performance…”). Advanced Analysis: Prompts that leverage the AI’s language capabilities, including: Analyzing and summarizing themes in open-ended written responses. Identifying patterns of misconception across different questions. Generating suggestions for curriculum adjustments based on student performance. Step 3: Actionable Insights: The final prompt focuses on converting the analysis into concrete, self-directed re-teaching strategies for students.

  1. Action Item

The Instructor will apply this refined three-step process to a new quiz dataset to test its effectiveness in a new context. Here are the meeting minutes from our professional development day, summarizing our discussion on creating a “Research Log” to make student thinking visible.

Meeting Minutes: Developing a Research Log Date: August 19, 2025

Topic: Integrating Science and Engineering Practices into a Research Log

Objective: To design a single, coherent “Research Log” that tracks student thinking and intellectual growth across all eight practices of science and engineering, with a particular emphasis on metacognition.

Key Decisions & Outcomes:

Guiding Framework: The group agreed to use a phenomenon-driven inquiry approach as the core of the log, starting each entry with a captivating real-world puzzle. Visible Thinking Activities: We designed three concise, relevant activities for each of the eight practices. These activities were created to directly complement our curriculum and were refined to be more concise throughout the session. Log Structure: We developed a sequential, phased structure for the Research Log to guide students from initial inquiry to final communication. The log will include dedicated sections and prompts for each stage of the scientific process. Inclusion of Metacognition: To track intellectual growth, we agreed to incorporate metacognitive check-ins at key transition points in the log. These prompts will ask students to reflect on their own understanding, changes in their models, and the evolution of their thinking. Final Conceptualization: The final concept for the log is a comprehensive tool that serves as a record of both the scientific process and the student’s journey through it. It begins with the simple “I notice…/I wonder…” and progresses to a final summary of their intellectual growth. Next Steps:

Formalize the table of contents for the Research Log. Draft the final prompts and questions for each section of the log. Pilot the log with a small group of students to gather initial feedback. Action Items:

Eleanor: Finalize the full draft of the Research Log’s content. Mr./Ms. [Teacher’s Name]: Review the full draft and provide feedback. Meeting Minutes: Curriculum & Workflow Iteration Date: [Current Date] Topic: Integrating Metacognitive Prompts into Natural Hazard Engineering Curriculum Initial Goal: To brainstorm “Research Briefs”—short, modifiable prompts for student reflection. Key Conceptual Shifts & Evolutions: From Brainstorming to Architectural Framework: The initial brainstorming evolved into defining a specific, three-part architecture for the briefs: “The Forecast” (pre-unit), “The Blueprint” (problem-solving), and “The Reflection” (post-unit). This provided a clear, repeatable structure. From Integration Strategy to Pragmatic Approach: We shifted from a general discussion of integration strategies (Unit-Specific, Routine & Rhythmic, Portfolio-Driven) to a focused decision. Given the constraints of a mixed-level class and a tight implementation deadline, we determined that the “Routine & Rhythmic” approach was the most practical and effective. From Ideal to Iterative: We recognized the difference between an ideal, comprehensive tool (like the provided research-log.html exemplar) and a practical, starting point. We affirmed that starting with a simple, concise, and repeatable workflow is key to success and can be iterated upon later. Final Determinations & Action Items: Final Framework: Implement the “Routine & Rhythmic” framework using the three-part brief architecture. Implementation Workflow: Adopt the developed five-step workflow for creating briefs for each unit. Final Briefs: Utilize the concise, sample prompts drafted in our conversation. Rationale: This workflow prioritizes beneficial predictability for students and implementation efficiency for the instructor, directly supporting the goal of fostering better learners. Meeting Minutes Date: August 19, 2025

Project: AI-Assisted Development of “Physics: A Story of Matter, Forces, and Energy” Flexbook

Attendees: Project Lead (High School Teacher), Eleanor Ainsworth (AI Assistant)

Objective:

To document the collaborative workflow and key developmental milestones in drafting a phenomenon-driven physics Flexbook. These minutes will serve as a basis for creating professional development materials for educators interested in similar AI-assisted curriculum projects.

Summary of Work The collaboration successfully produced eleven detailed chapter “storylines” for a new physics Flexbook. The process was iterative, with the AI generating chapter drafts based on an initial framework provided by the Project Lead. The core pedagogical model—anchoring each chapter in a real-world phenomenon and aligning with NGSS principles—was maintained throughout.

Key Process Milestones & Shifts Initial Framework & Onboarding: The project began with the Project Lead providing a comprehensive guiding document. The AI successfully assimilated this framework, establishing a consistent, high-quality output from the first chapter. Feedback Integration & Narrative Enrichment: A notable shift occurred following the drafting of Chapter 5. The Project Lead requested a greater emphasis on historical context and the human stories behind the science. This feedback was immediately and effectively incorporated into all subsequent chapters (6-10), enriching the narrative with figures like Maxwell, Planck, and de Broglie. Human Oversight & Course Correction: A critical interaction involved the AI inadvertently skipping Chapter 9 and drafting Chapter 10. The Project Lead identified the error, and the AI seamlessly corrected the sequence. This event underscores the essential role of human supervision in maintaining the structural integrity and logical flow of the curriculum. Shift from Drafting to Dialogue: The creation of the concluding chapter (Chapter 11) marked a significant evolution in the collaborative method. Rather than a simple draft request, the conclusion was co-created through a Socratic dialogue. The AI posed a series of targeted questions, using the Project Lead’s philosophical input to shape a final chapter focused on responsibility and rational hope. Takeaways for Professional Development The Power of a Strong Framework: A clear, upfront vision and pedagogical framework are critical for guiding the AI and ensuring a coherent final product. AI as a “First Draft” Accelerator: The AI assistant proved exceptionally effective at rapidly generating well-structured, narratively compelling first drafts, drastically reducing development time. The Educator as Director: The human expert’s role is not one of a mere prompter, but of a director—guiding the narrative, fact-checking, identifying structural issues, and providing qualitative feedback to refine the tone and content. Dialogue Unlocks Deeper Collaboration: Moving beyond simple commands to a more conversational, question-based interaction can yield a final product that is more deeply aligned with the educator’s personal pedagogical voice and vision. Of course. Based on our work, here are four action steps that would synthesize the individual storylines into a more cohesive and impactful book:

  1. Weave the “Human Element” Throughline Our work improved significantly when we began incorporating the historical figures and narratives from Chapter 6 onward. A key next step is to retrofit Chapters 1-5 with this same “human element.” For instance, when discussing standards in Chapter 1, we can briefly introduce the French scientists who established the metric system. When introducing kinematics in Chapter 2, we can touch upon Galileo’s foundational experiments. This will create a consistent narrative voice and reinforce the idea that science is a dynamic, human story from the very beginning.

  2. Explicitly Cross-Reference the “Thinking Lenses” We introduced a powerful new “Thinking Lens” (NGSS Crosscutting Concept) in each chapter. To create a more integrated text, we should now go back and explicitly connect these lenses across chapters. For example, the conclusion of the chapter on momentum (Chapter 4, Lens: Systems) could foreshadow the chapter on energy (Chapter 5, Lens: Energy and Matter) by posing a question like, “While momentum is conserved within this system, what other quantity must we account for to tell the whole story?” This will help students see these concepts not as isolated tools, but as an interconnected way of thinking.

  3. Bridge the Classical/Quantum Divide There is a significant conceptual leap between the classical physics of the early chapters and the quantum mechanics of the later ones. We should create a “bridge” by seeding the later classical chapters with the puzzles that led to the quantum revolution. The chapter on light (Chapter 7) is the perfect place to more strongly emphasize the “ultraviolet catastrophe” as an unsolved mystery, making its resolution by Max Planck in Chapter 8 a more satisfying and logical next step. This turns the chapter sequence into a compelling mystery and its solution.

  4. Harmonize with the Final Message Our collaboratively-written conclusion (Chapter 11) establishes a powerful theme of “rational hope and responsibility.” The final action step is to review and subtly revise the “Putting It Together” sections of each chapter to align with this theme. For example, after explaining the physics of a crumple zone (Chapter 4), we can add a sentence that touches on the social responsibility of engineers. After explaining the hydroelectric dam (Chapter 5), we can briefly mention the environmental considerations. This ensures that the book’s final, powerful message feels earned and has been built incrementally throughout the entire text.

Meeting Minutes Session: Professional Development: Curriculum Pacing Adaptation Date: August 19, 2025 Topic: Adapting the Physics Curriculum to the 2025-26 Bell Schedule Facilitator: Eleanor Ainsworth (Curriculum & Instruction Designer)

Objective To analyze the new 2025-2026 academic calendar and “8 drop 2” bell schedule, and to adapt the existing year-long Physics curriculum into a new, week-by-week pacing guide.

Discussion & Key Findings Document Review: The session began with a systematic review of three core documents: the BPS Academic Calendar, the new BHS Bell Schedule, and the previous year’s Physics curriculum breakdown. Schedule Analysis & Clarification: The new “8 drop 2” schedule operates on a 4-day rotation. A critical point of clarification was established: analysis of the schedule confirmed that any given class meets 3 times per 4-day cycle. This corrected an initial misconception and provided a foundational understanding for pacing. Instructional Time Analysis: A high-level comparison of total instructional time was conducted. The new schedule provides approximately 132 total contact hours over the academic year. This represents a minor decrease from the estimated ~135 hours of a traditional A/B block schedule, highlighting that the primary challenge is adapting to a new cadence (more frequent but shorter meetings) rather than a significant loss of time. Outcomes & Next Steps Visual Pacing Guide Generated: A comprehensive, week-by-week infographic was created, mapping the Physics curriculum units and key assessments onto the new 4-day rotation for the entire school year. Action Item: The instructor is to review the generated pacing guide infographic for content flow and feasibility. Further consultation can be scheduled to adjust the placement of specific topics or assessments as needed. Of course. Here are the follow-up meeting minutes.

Meeting Minutes: Physics Curriculum Development PD (Follow-up) Date: August 19, 2025

Topic: Data Management for Curriculum Infographics

Objective:

Following the successful creation of the curriculum infographic, today’s objective was to improve the long-term maintainability and efficiency of our digital resources.

Summary of Progress:

Identifying an Efficiency: We recognized that hard-coding the curriculum data directly into the infographic’s HTML structure would be inefficient for future updates. Any change to the curriculum would require editing the code directly. Key Decision - Data Externalization: To address this, we decided to separate the curriculum content from its visual presentation. The most effective solution was to structure all the curriculum information into a single, well-organized data file. Action Item Completed: A comprehensive JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) file was drafted. This file now serves as the single source of truth for all curriculum details, including part titles, unit descriptions, core ideas, key skills, anchoring phenomena, and crosscutting concepts. Next Steps:

The new JSON file is complete and ready for use. Future development work will involve connecting this data file to our visual infographics. This will allow any updates to the JSON file to be automatically reflected in our digital resources, ensuring consistency and simplifying future revisions.
